content: When responding to a confirmed outbreak of wild poliovirus (WPV) or vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV), it is critical to investigate any suspected outbreak immediately to confirm its presence or determine if there is a high enough suspicion to justify an immunization response. If an outbreak is confirmed, the country must notify the World Health Organization (WHO) within 24 hours. The Ministry of Health, through its immunization services or a specialized steering group of experts, should provide guidance and coordinate nationwide response activities. The response must align with the current WHO guidelines for outbreak management. Individuals with primary immunodeficiency disorders (PIDs), which are genetically inherited conditions affecting the B-cell system, may experience prolonged intestinal replication and shedding of poliovirus beyond the usual 4–6 weeks. This extended shedding can lead to the emergence of vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs). When VDPVs evolve in PID patients following exposure to oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) strains, they are classified as immunodeficiency-related vaccine-derived polioviruses (iVDPVs). To mitigate the risks posed by iVDPVs to both individuals and communities during the polio endgame and post-eradication era, it is essential to identify PID patients excreting polioviruses and develop strategies to eliminate the associated risks. Acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance can only detect poliovirus transmission through cases of paralysis. While environmental surveillance (ES) can identify iVDPV shedding by asymptomatic carriers, it cannot pinpoint the individual excreting the virus. Therefore, supplementary systems are needed to identify all poliovirus excretors, eradicate the virus, and maintain eradication. The primary objective of surveillance is to identify PID patients excreting poliovirus before the virus causes paralysis or initiates community transmission. Surveillance should also guide effective case management protocols and propose public health responses to reduce the risk of poliomyelitis in individuals and prevent poliovirus transmission in the community. A PID patient at risk of poliovirus excretion is defined as an individual of any age with a primary antibody disorder, humoral (B-cell), or combined humoral and cellular (T-cell) immunodeficiency disorder, confirmed to have immunoglobulin levels below the age-appropriate standard. Specific PIDs associated with prolonged poliovirus excretion include common variable immunodeficiency disorder, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency disorder, and other immunodeficiencies with hypogammaglobulinemia or increased susceptibility to viral infections. Surveillance programs will identify two types of cases: individuals previously diagnosed with a PID who meet the case definition, identified through retrospective searches of national and facility registries, and newly diagnosed PID patients known to be associated with prolonged poliovirus excretion, who will be screened for poliovirus shortly after diagnosis. PID patients with confirmed poliovirus excretion are those at risk of prolonged shedding, whose stool specimens test positive for WPV, VDPV, or Sabin-like viruses. These cases are classified based on the serotype of the isolated virus (e.g., iVDPV1, WPV1, SL1). PID patients with no laboratory evidence of poliovirus in adequate stool specimens are classified as negative for poliovirus. If paralysis is present at the time of PID diagnosis, the case should be reported as an AFP case to the polio surveillance officer and investigated according to AFP surveillance guidelines. Stool samples should be tested for poliovirus as soon as possible after the onset of paralysis, and cases should be classified according to AFP guidelines. PID patients with AFP should also be included in the PID surveillance database for coordinated treatment, contact sampling, and follow-up. Treatment with antiviral drugs should be considered for PID patients if VDPV is isolated in their stool specimens, if they have been excreting Sabin strains for more than two months, or if they are excreting WPV. Antivirals are not indicated for contacts potentially exposed to poliovirus. The clinical immunologist or specialist physician attending to the PID patient should coordinate with surveillance officers and public health authorities to decide on treatment and follow-up procedures. The patient and their family should be counseled to avoid live vaccines in the future and maintain proper hygiene to prevent poliovirus transmission. Health staff should be vaccinated with inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) and adhere to infection control precautions. Close contacts of the patient should also be vaccinated with IPV, if required, but should not receive OPV. Surveillance data are essential for detecting and monitoring PID patients with prolonged poliovirus excretion, treating infections, preventing paralysis, and recording the number and location of poliovirus excretors. Data sources include case investigation forms, follow-up forms, PID patient registries, and active surveillance visit forms. Epidemiological analysis should include the number of PID patients at risk of poliovirus excretion, the number of patients with negative or prolonged Sabin excretion, and other relevant metrics.
